newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia protests at Turkish threats against Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Russia protests at Turkish threats against Cyprus.

text.p: Russia protested on Saturday at Turkish threats of military action against Cyprus, which came after Moscow agreed to sell missiles to the Greek Cypriot government.

Russia "cannot ignore such statements from Turkey, including a direct threat against the safety of the sovereign Republic of Cyprus," Foreign Ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov said in a written statement.

Turkey on Friday repeated its threat to take military action against Cyprus to stop it from deploying the Russian missiles and said it might occupy an abandoned tourist resort on the island if the Greek Cypriot government did not back down.
"Such a statement seems especially strange considering the evident fact that the S-300 anti-aircraft missile system is of a purely defensive character," Tarasov said.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said Turkey could knock out the system the Greek Cypriot government plans to install under a deal made with Russia last weekend.
"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," Ciller told reporters.
Russia said such remarks lessened the possibility of reaching a solution to the tensions on the island.

"The artificial aggravation of tensions can only delay the future settlement of the Cyprus problem, and it does not help stability or improve the atmosphere of trust and cooperation in the region," Tarasov said.

The United States and west European governments have condemned the sale of the weapons system, angering Moscow which says the West is simply trying to prevent Russia taking a greater share of the world arms market.
Saturday's foreign ministry statement also reiterated Russia's call for a full demilitarisation of Cyprus.

Turkey has about 30,000 troops in the northern third of Cyprus which declared itself a Turkish Cypriot state but is only recognised by Ankara. The internationally recognised Greek Cypriot government in the south commands a national guard of more than 10,000 troops and is backed militarily by Athens.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded northern Cyprus after a short-lived coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
